title: 06 — Lakeflow: Connect, Pipelines and Jobs
html:
06 — Lakeflow: Connect, Pipelines and Jobs

The one idea: Lakeflow splits data engineering into three managed pieces. Connect brings data in, declarative pipelines turn it into tables you describe rather than script, and Jobs run everything on schedules and triggers. You write what the tables should contain; the platform handles order, retries, checkpoints and history.

1. What it is

Piece Former name Job
Lakeflow Connect (new) Managed connectors from databases (for example SQL Server through change tracking or CDC), SaaS apps and files into Unity Catalog streaming tables
Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines Delta Live Tables (DLT) Declare streaming tables, materialized views and flows in SQL or Python. The engine builds the dependency graph and runs it
Lakeflow Jobs Workflows Orchestrate tasks (notebooks, pipelines, SQL, Python, dbt and more), with triggers, retries, conditions and loops

The open-source side has moved too. Spark Declarative Pipelines arrived in Apache Spark 4.1, with Python and SQL authoring and a CLI. A secondary 2026 source says Spark 4.2 adds a SQL CHANGES clause and Auto CDC. Spark 4.1 also introduced Real-Time Mode for Structured Streaming: very low latency, and in 4.1 limited to stateless queries, with stateful support planned for a later release.

2. Why it matters

  • CDC done right is hard: out-of-order events, duplicates, deletes and history. AUTO CDC does it declaratively.
  • Expectations give per-row quality rules with warn, drop or fail behaviour, and record metrics.
  • Event-driven runs (file arrival, table update) remove polling and late batches.
  • Bundles put all of it in Git and deploy it the same way to dev, test and prod.

3. The main ideas

3.1 Datasets in a declarative pipeline

Dataset Behaviour Typical use
Streaming table Processes each new input once (append or AUTO CDC) Bronze ingestion, CDC targets
Materialized view Kept up to date with its query, incrementally where possible Silver and Gold aggregates
View (temporary) Named query inside the pipeline Intermediate steps
Flow A query that writes into a target. Several flows can feed one target Merging several sources into one table

Python authoring uses from pyspark import pipelines as dp, with decorators such as @dp.table, @dp.materialized_view and @dp.expect_or_drop. SQL uses CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE and CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW.

3.2 AUTO CDC and SCD Type 2

AUTO CDC (formerly APPLY CHANGES) takes a stream of change events and maintains a target table:

  • KEYS: the business key.
  • SEQUENCE BY: the column that orders events. Arrival order is ignored, so late events land in the right place.
  • APPLY AS DELETE WHEN: which events are deletes.
  • STORED AS SCD TYPE 1 keeps only the latest row. SCD TYPE 2 keeps history with __START_AT and __END_AT columns.
  • Release notes from 2025 added a name parameter, so several AUTO CDC flows can write to one target, plus a once option for one-time backfills and SQL CREATE FLOW ... AUTO CDC INTO.
-- Not run: requires a Lakeflow pipeline. Column names are made up.
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE silver.fund_manager_history;

CREATE FLOW fund_manager_cdc AS AUTO CDC INTO silver.fund_manager_history
FROM STREAM(bronze.fund_manager_changes)
KEYS (fund_id)
APPLY AS DELETE WHEN operation = 'DELETE'
SEQUENCE BY change_seq
COLUMNS * EXCEPT (operation, change_seq)
STORED AS SCD TYPE 2;

SCD2 is not the same as bitemporal. __START_AT and __END_AT follow the sequence column, which is usually when the source changed it. If you also need when we learned it, keep a separate knowledge-time column, as the storage module explains.

3.3 Jobs: tasks, triggers and control flow

---
title: Lakeflow Jobs — one job, event-driven
---
flowchart LR
    TRG["Trigger<br/>file arrival in a volume"] --> T1["Task 1: pipeline<br/>bronze to silver"]
    T1 --> C{"Condition task<br/>rows quarantined = 0?"}
    C -- "true" --> T2["Task 2: publish<br/>(SQL)"]
    C -- "false" --> T3["Task 3: notify owner"]
    T2 --> FE["For each task<br/>refresh 6 product tables"]
  • Triggers (per the docs, checked 2026-10-26): scheduled, table update, file arrival in a UC storage location, model update, continuous, or manual.
  • Control flow: dependencies, if/else condition tasks, for each tasks over a list, run-job tasks.
  • Reliability: retries per task, timeouts, repair run (re-run only failed tasks), and max concurrent runs (default one).

3.4 Bundles

Databricks Asset Bundles were renamed Declarative Automation Bundles on 16 March 2026, per the release notes. The CLI commands and existing configuration keep working. A bundle (databricks.yml) describes jobs, pipelines, apps, dashboards and permissions as code, with targets (dev, staging, prod). databricks bundle validate, deploy and run are the CI/CD steps.

4. Working code

The script reproduces what AUTO CDC with SCD Type 2 does with late and duplicate events. Standard library only.

# What a declarative "AUTO CDC ... SEQUENCE BY ... STORED AS SCD TYPE 2" flow does for you, in miniature.
# Change events can arrive late and out of order. The sequence column, not arrival order, decides history.
events = [  # (key, sequence, operation, payload) in ARRIVAL order
    ("FUND-1", 3, "UPSERT", {"manager": "K. Shah"}),
    ("FUND-1", 1, "UPSERT", {"manager": "A. Rao"}),
    ("FUND-2", 1, "UPSERT", {"manager": "S. Iyer"}),
    ("FUND-1", 2, "UPSERT", {"manager": "P. Nair"}),     # late: belongs between seq 1 and seq 3
    ("FUND-2", 2, "DELETE", None),
    ("FUND-1", 3, "UPSERT", {"manager": "K. Shah"}),     # duplicate delivery of seq 3
]

def scd2(events):
    latest = {}
    for key, seq, op, payload in events:                  # keep one event per (key, sequence): duplicates vanish
        latest[(key, seq)] = (op, payload)
    history = []
    for key in sorted({k for k, _ in latest}):
        versions = sorted((s, *latest[(k, s)]) for k, s in latest if k == key)
        for i, (seq, op, payload) in enumerate(versions):
            if op == "DELETE":
                continue
            end = versions[i + 1][0] if i + 1 < len(versions) else None
            history.append({"key": key, **payload, "__START_AT": seq, "__END_AT": end})
    return history

for row in scd2(events):
    print(row)

Output:

{'key': 'FUND-1', 'manager': 'A. Rao', '__START_AT': 1, '__END_AT': 2}
{'key': 'FUND-1', 'manager': 'P. Nair', '__START_AT': 2, '__END_AT': 3}
{'key': 'FUND-1', 'manager': 'K. Shah', '__START_AT': 3, '__END_AT': None}
{'key': 'FUND-2', 'manager': 'S. Iyer', '__START_AT': 1, '__END_AT': 2}

What to notice:

  • Sequence 2 for FUND-1 arrived after sequence 3, but history is still ordered 1 → 2 → 3, because SEQUENCE BY decides, not arrival order.
  • The duplicate delivery of sequence 3 produced no extra version.
  • FUND-2's delete closed its only version (__END_AT = 2) instead of erasing it.

5. Common mistakes

  1. Sequencing by ingestion time. Late events then overwrite newer ones. Sequence by the source's own change order.
  2. Expecting SCD2 to answer "as we knew it". It records the source's change time. Add knowledge time yourself.
  3. Cron polling for files. Use a file-arrival trigger, and check its documented limits.
  4. One giant notebook task. Split it into tasks, so repair runs re-execute only what failed.
  5. Clicking jobs together in the UI for production. Define them in a bundle, so they are reviewed, versioned and repeatable.

6. Exercise (2 hours)

  1. Extend the script with SCD Type 1 output, and with a TRUNCATE event that closes every open version.
  2. On Databricks Free Edition (one active pipeline per type is allowed), build a two-table pipeline: a streaming table from a volume of CSV files, and a materialized view with one expect_or_drop rule.
  3. Write a databricks.yml with a dev and a prod target for that pipeline and a job that runs it on file arrival.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. What does SEQUENCE BY protect you from?
  2. What are __START_AT and __END_AT, and what do they not tell you?
  3. Name four Lakeflow Jobs trigger types.
  4. What happened to Databricks Asset Bundles in March 2026?
  5. What is Spark 4.1 Real-Time Mode limited to?

Answers

  1. Late and out-of-order events overwriting newer data.
  2. The SCD2 validity range by sequence value. They don't record when your platform learned the change.
  3. Any four of: scheduled, table update, file arrival, model update, continuous (plus manual).
  4. They were renamed Declarative Automation Bundles. Commands and configuration were unchanged.
  5. Stateless queries such as projections, filters, unions and stream-static joins.

8. Sources
